rascalz.bio:
Formed in Vancouver in the early 1990s, Rascalz became one of the most consequential groups in the development of Canadian hip-hop outside Toronto. Built around MCs Red1 and Misfit and DJ Kemo, with breakers Zebroc and Dedos part of the wider crew, the group treated MCing, DJing, graffiti and breaking as connected parts of hip-hop culture. They first recorded as Ragga Muffin Rascals before releasing Really Livin', then reached a much larger national audience with 1997's Cash Crop, a record that established the West Coast as a serious centre of Canadian rap rather than a regional afterthought.

Cash Crop won the 1998 JUNO for Best Rap Recording, but Rascalz refused the award because the rap category was presented during the non-televised portion of the ceremony. Their protest drew attention to the marginalization of Black music within Canada's biggest music awards, and the following year the rap award moved onto the televised broadcast. Rascalz then returned with "Northern Touch," produced by Kemo and featuring Checkmate, Kardinal Offishall, Thrust and Choclair. The cross-country posse cut became a landmark Canadian rap anthem, won the 1999 JUNO and was performed on the broadcast, giving the country's hip-hop community a rare national showcase at a moment when domestic rap still struggled for mainstream infrastructure.

The group followed with Global Warning in 1999 and Reloaded in the early 2000s, but Rascalz's lasting significance rests as much on what they changed around the music as on their catalogue. "Northern Touch" linked Vancouver and Toronto scenes into a shared national statement, while the JUNO protest challenged an industry practice that had kept rap out of prime view. Together, those moments made Rascalz a bridge between Canada's underground hip-hop networks and the more visible national ecosystem that followed, and established Vancouver as an essential part of that history.
rascalz.directory_summary: Vancouver's Rascalz helped move Canadian hip-hop from regional underground scenes toward a national conversation. Their 1997 album Cash Crop won a JUNO, but the group refused the award to protest rap's exclusion from the televised ceremony. A year later, the cross-country posse cut "Northern Touch" united Rascalz with Checkmate, Kardinal Offishall, Thrust and Choclair, won the 1999 JUNO and became one of Canadian rap's defining anthems. Their impact joined strong records with an industry-changing demand that hip-hop receive serious national visibility.

muzion.bio:
Formed in Montréal in 1996 by J.Kyll, Imposs and Dramatik, Muzion became one of the foundational groups of Québec hip-hop by making the city's Haitian diaspora central to the music rather than peripheral to it. The trio moved naturally among French, English and Haitian Creole, bringing the language and experience of neighbourhoods including Saint-Michel into a Québec rap landscape that was still defining itself. Their 1999 debut Mentalité moune morne… (Ils n'ont pas compris) paired dense, socially engaged writing with a distinctly Montréal perspective and won the Félix for Hip-Hop Album of the Year, establishing Muzion as both a critical force and a cultural point of identification for Black and immigrant audiences in Québec.

Their second album, J'rêvolutionne, followed in 2002 and also earned a Félix for Hip-Hop Album of the Year. The group's most enduring anthem, "La vi ti nèg," fused hip-hop with kompa and celebrated Haitian life in Montréal with a combination of resilience, neighbourhood pride and joy. The song won a Canadian Urban Music Award in 2004, and its influence continued long after Muzion's initial recording run: in 2025, SOCAN gave "La vi ti nèg" its Cultural Impact Award, the first time the honour had gone to a hip-hop song in the gala's history. Artists from later generations of Québec rap have repeatedly identified Muzion as proof that their own communities, accents and cultural references could belong in the province's mainstream music conversation.

That legacy received another national acknowledgement in January 2026, when Canada Post honoured Muzion alongside Maestro Fresh Wes and Michie Mee in a Black History Month stamp series celebrating Canadian hip-hop trailblazers. For Northern Dial, Muzion matters because they connect several histories at once: the rise of francophone rap, Montréal's Haitian cultural presence, women in Québec hip-hop through J.Kyll's visibility, and a broader Canadian story in which local identity became a source of musical authority rather than something artists had to dilute to be heard.
muzion.directory_summary: Montréal trio Muzion made Haitian-Québécois identity foundational to the sound and language of late-1990s Québec hip-hop. J.Kyll, Imposs and Dramatik moved among French, English and Haitian Creole on the Félix-winning albums Mentalité moune morne… (Ils n'ont pas compris) and J'rêvolutionne. Their kompa-inflected anthem "La vi ti nèg" later received SOCAN's Cultural Impact Award, while Canada Post honoured the group in its 2026 Canadian hip-hop stamp series. Muzion's influence helped later Black and immigrant artists see their own neighbourhoods and cultural references reflected in Québec music.

william prince.bio:
William Prince grew up on Peguis First Nation in Manitoba, where music first functioned less as entertainment than as service. His father was a preacher and musician, and Prince learned to accompany him on guitar while travelling to First Nations communities and singing at church services, wakes and funerals. That background shaped the measured pace, deep baritone and sense of emotional responsibility that became central to his songwriting. His debut album Earthly Days introduced that voice nationally and won the 2017 JUNO for Contemporary Roots Album of the Year, turning a regional Manitoba singer-songwriter into one of Canada's most distinctive new roots artists.

Prince expanded that foundation rather than abandoning it. Reliever developed his folk-country writing on a broader production scale, while the 2020 companion project Gospel First Nation returned directly to the hymns, communities and contradictions of the Christian tradition in which he was raised. Stand in the Joy continued the arc in 2023 with songs built around love, family and survival rather than treating Indigenous identity as a fixed subject category. Across that catalogue, Prince has earned two JUNO Awards, received the John Prine Songwriter Fellowship and appeared on stages ranging from NPR's Tiny Desk to the Newport Folk Festival, building an international audience without separating his work from Peguis and the Manitoba Interlake.

His fifth album, Further From the Country, arrived in October 2025 and widened the sonic frame with a more expansive band while returning to questions of distance, grief, identity and what it means to leave home without severing it. The record's title captures the tension running through Prince's career: his music has travelled far beyond the community where he learned to play, but its power still comes from the restraint, storytelling and communal purpose formed there. In Canadian roots music, Prince represents a contemporary Indigenous songwriting voice that can sit naturally beside country, gospel, folk and Americana traditions while remaining unmistakably grounded in his own place and experience.
william prince.directory_summary: Peguis First Nation singer-songwriter William Prince built his resonant folk-country style from music learned alongside his preacher father at church services, wakes and funerals across Manitoba. His debut Earthly Days won the 2017 JUNO for Contemporary Roots Album of the Year, beginning a catalogue that later included Reliever, Gospel First Nation, Stand in the Joy and 2025's Further From the Country. A two-time JUNO winner and John Prine Songwriter Fellowship recipient, Prince pairs a commanding baritone with restrained writing about family, grief, place and the distance between home and a growing international career.
